newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Brash comments send NZ dlr to sharply lower close.
newsitem.headline: Brash comments send NZ dlr to sharply lower close.

text.p: The New Zealand dollar ended sharply weaker on Thursday on comments by Reserve Bank Governor Don Brash and amid nervousness that the offshore market may take the currency lower overnight.

The Kiwi was closed locally at 5 p.m. (0400 GMT) at US$0.7050/57 and 67.04 on its Trade-Weighted Index, from an opening 0.7121/28 and 67.79, and having traded a 0.7047-7125 range. Shortly before 0500 GMT, however, it had slipped to 0.7024/31 and 66.84.
The sell-off was sparked mid-afternoon by a Brash comment to reporters at an exporters' summit in Wellington.
"I have often suggested the exchange rate goes through cycles -- the real exchange rate, particularly, goes through cycles. At the moment it's in the top of one of those cycles," Brash said.

Although his speech to the conference was off the record, the head of rural lobby Federated Farmers later said he believed Brash was comfortable with some flexibility in the central bank's zero to two percent inflation target over the course of the business cycle.
The currency sold off more than 40 basis points on the remarks, but a senior dealer said there was reasonable two-way business and some exporter interest to buy at the lower levels.
"My main concern would be the reaction of the offshore markets when they come in," he said.

He said fund managers might well be prompted to sell by the Brash comments and continuing political vacuum, although caretaker Prime Minister Jim Bolger said parliament would meet on December 12 for the first time since the October election.
The caretaker National Party government and Labour are both trying to clinch a coalition deal with nationalist New Zealand First before parliament meets.
Offshore investors were already quite bearish and a lot had been looking to sell, an Auckland dealer said. "They make take this as the signal to do it."
He said rumours of an end to New Zealand dollar samurai issues were a further source of weakness.
He said 70 U.S. cents should hold overnight but "stranger things have happened".
